title: HIIT
subtitle: Choose an effort you can manage and make recovery part of your fitness plan.

blocks.text: A fitness app can announce a personal best before you’ve found both shoes. Its enthusiasm is free, but it can’t decide which effort fits your day. This lesson helps you choose intervals with a clear purpose and enough recovery.
Get fitter in less time, at a pace that fits you.
blocks.detail: Knowing the difference between moderate intervals and HIIT lets you pick a session that matches your energy and builds fitness without burning out.
blocks.extra: Section 05 walks you through a full session, minute by minute.

blocks.text: An interval is a planned stretch of activity followed by an easier stretch. You might walk briskly for a short time, then slow down before repeating. Switching speeds alone doesn’t make a session high intensity.

High-intensity interval training, or HIIT, mixes short bursts of vigorous effort with easier recovery. Vigorous means hard for you, not a fixed speed everyone must reach. HIIT doesn’t require all-out sprinting. Research, including work at McMaster University in Hamilton, shows HIIT can improve heart and lung fitness as much as longer moderate sessions, in less time. It’s harder, though, and you don’t need it to be healthy.

This is general adult education, not a personal prescription. Fill out CSEP’s Get Active Questionnaire. A yes answer means follow its extra guidance, not that you’re banned. Keep private health answers off this worksheet.

Start with an activity you can control, such as walking on a clear, level route or riding a stationary bike. A bike raises effort without jumping, but the seat and controls still need to fit you. Low impact describes the movement, not how hard your heart and lungs work.
Check effort without chasing a number

During moderate activity, you can usually talk but not sing comfortably. Vigorous activity makes your breathing faster and talking harder. These are clues, not a medical test. Unusual symptoms fall under the stop rules in Section 05.
Use your own pace. The same walking speed may feel easy to one person and hard to another. Choose your effort by how your body responds, not by a neighbour’s speed or an app’s leaderboard.

Recovery means slowing down enough to regain control before the next effort. If you still feel rushed when the timer goes off, stretch the easy part or end the rounds. A countdown is a planning tool, and it has never met your knees.
Count the whole session. Include the warm-up, every recovery and the cool-down when you book time. Six short efforts can need a much longer visit than the headline suggests.

items.title: “A session only counts if it leaves me exhausted.”
items.text: Moderate activity builds fitness too. Finishing with control is a good aim, and HIIT is an option, not a requirement.

blocks.text: If you’re new to exercise or coming back after a long break, start with easy or moderate activity. Build a steady routine before you try HIIT, and get qualified advice if you’re not sure you’re ready. Being in an advanced lesson doesn’t mean you start at an advanced level.

For adults aged 18 to 64, Canada’s guidelines include at least 150 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity a week and muscle strengthening at least twice a week. A short interval session is one part of a broader routine, not the whole plan.

sections.title: Fictional learning story: The lunch break

blocks.text: The lunch break
paragraphs: Omar worked at a library in Winnipeg. He wanted a workout that fit his lunch break and gave him more energy for evening walks with his partner. His phone kept advertising a ten-minute workout while his lunch sat waiting on the counter.

When the library offered a deal at the rec centre, Omar booked a first visit. He walked a lot but had never tried intervals. The bike screen showed a bright Race Mode, and he almost picked it, since it looked like the right way to start.

A trainer asked about his goals and checked that he was ready before they talked about harder work. Omar saw that Race Mode gave him almost no time to catch his breath. He had a choice: chase the score, or learn a pace he could manage.

He chose the easier plan. After a slow start, he pedalled hard for short bursts with longer easy stretches in between, then cooled down. He could still talk during the hard parts and felt ready before each one.

The surprise came when he checked the clock. Changing, warming up and cooling down made the visit far longer than the ten minutes in the ad. Instead of cutting his rest, he moved his gym visits to quiet afternoons and kept his lunch breaks for walks.

For several visits, Omar repeated the same plan while he learned the bike. He decided to talk about harder intervals later, with no deadline. His phone still offered ten-minute miracles, but now his calendar showed the whole visit, and his lunch got eaten.

blocks.text: Write down one useful detail: whether recovery felt long enough and whether the session fit your day. Those notes will help you choose better next time than a score alone.
Plan the whole visit, and the habit will stick.
blocks.detail: Leaving time for warm-up and recovery makes your sessions fit a real day, so you keep coming back.
blocks.extra: Section 05 gives you a starter session you can try this week.

blocks.text: Choose a clear space, familiar equipment and enough time before you start. Check local conditions. Ice, heat or wildfire smoke may call for an indoor option with good air. Keep water nearby and learn how to slow or stop the machine.
Adjustable learning example: moderate starter
This example teaches timing and isn’t a personal prescription. Use comfortable walking or a stationary bike, with moderate efforts. It’s an interval starter, not HIIT.

items.title: Warm up: 5 minutes of easy movement.
Repeat 4 times: 30 seconds at moderate effort, then 90 seconds easy.
Cool down: 5 minutes of easy movement.

blocks.text: Recovery is included after the last effort. Four rounds contain 2 minutes of moderate work and 6 minutes easy. Do not label all 18 minutes as vigorous exercise.

If it’s too much, do fewer rounds or stay easy the whole time. Longer recovery also changes the total: four rounds of 30 seconds moderate and 2 minutes easy make a 20-minute session with the same warm-up and cool-down. You can repeat a comfortable version with no deadline.
Where HIIT fits

Someone already active and ready for vigorous exercise could talk with a qualified exercise professional about a HIIT version. Turning the short work periods into controlled vigorous effort changes the intensity, even if the clock stays the same. One well-studied example from McMaster University is 10 rounds of 1 minute hard and 1 minute easy, with a warm-up and cool-down. Avoid all-out effort, and leave easier days between hard sessions.

Change one thing. Once a version feels manageable over several sessions, think about changing the effort, the number of rounds or the length. Keep everything else the same so you can judge how you respond.

items.title: “Less recovery always makes a better workout.”
items.text: If the next effort starts before you’ve regained control, more recovery or fewer rounds may be the useful change.

blocks.text: Insider tip: Set a gentle timer sound and label the easy periods. A notification called Recovery gives clearer instructions than a dramatic alarm that suggests the stationary bike is on fire.

Stop for chest pain or pressure, feeling faint, or severe or unusual breathlessness. Call 911 for chest pain, fainting or severe trouble breathing. Stop for pain that changes how you move, and get advice.
Quick Check

items.title: Does alternating easy and moderate walking automatically count as HIIT?
items.text: HIIT includes vigorous work periods; this starter stays moderate.

items.title: How long is the four-round moderate starter, including preparation and finish?
items.text: 5 minutes, 8 minutes of rounds and 5 minutes.

items.title: What should you do if recovery is still incomplete when the timer sounds?
items.detail: Extend the easy period or end the rounds rather than force the next effort.

blocks.text: Knowledge Check

items.title: Lee is returning after a long break. What is the best first choice? A. All-out bike sprints. · B. Easy or moderate activity with readiness checked. · C. The fastest class available.
items.text: Learn your response before considering vigorous intervals.

items.title: Ari needs longer to recover. What is a useful response? A. Ignore the timer and add recovery. · B. Skip the warm-up. · C. Increase speed to catch up.
items.text: Extend recovery when you need it.

items.title: Sam feels comfortable with the same session over repeated visits. What helps assess a change? A. Increase every setting. · B. Follow a stranger’s score. · C. Change one variable and review the response.
items.text: One change is easier to assess. You can also repeat a version.

items.title: Write two sentences explaining how you would make an interval session fit your day and current ability.
items.text: I will use moderate walking intervals on a clear indoor route and book time for the whole session. I will extend recovery or reduce rounds if I cannot regain control.

blocks.text: Choose intensity from your current readiness, leave room for recovery and count the whole session. Moderate intervals are a valid starting choice.
Write your own plan with a clear starting point and a recovery rule. If you’re not sure you’re ready, make getting advice your next step.
Check your plan’s total time and explain why you chose your effort level.

items.title: Interval
items.text: A planned period of movement or recovery.

items.title: HIIT
items.text: Short vigorous work periods separated by easier recovery.

items.title: Moderate effort
items.text: Activity during which you can generally talk but not sing comfortably.

items.title: Vigorous effort
items.text: Hard activity that makes breathing faster and conversation harder.

items.title: Recovery
items.text: Easier movement or rest between work periods.

items.title: Low impact
items.text: Movement with little pounding or jumping; effort can still be high.
